ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: 🌍 Almannagjá

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: We are walking down inside the crack. The wall on your left is the edge of North America.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: Most plate boundaries sit invisible under two kilometres of ocean. Here you can **walk into the one the planet is tearing open.**

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: Hand on the wall to your left: North America. It is going that way. You are going that way. Slowly, and there is no hurry — it is about as fast as your fingernails grow.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: Walking Into the Gap

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you are standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here. The valley **is** the gap.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: The cracks have names. **Almannagjá**, the big one you are walking through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it is the seam, still ripping.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: It does not creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the assembly ground.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m.** The parliament you are about to stand in met noticeably higher up than the ground you are on.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: 🎬 **On screen:** this gorge is the pass to the **Bloody Gate** in *Game of Thrones* — the gate was added digitally above the Öxarárfoss trail — and the park doubled as an otherworldly realm in ***Thor: The Dark World*** (2013).

ctx: gloss for the name "Þingvallahraun" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: the 9,000-year-old lava plain the valley floor is made of

ctx: gloss for the name "Skjaldbreiður" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá
en: the shield volcano that poured it out

ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
en: ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
en: At the Law Rock — the wall behind you is the reason this spot was chosen.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
en: In **930 CE**, Iceland's chieftains gathered here and founded the **Alþingi** — the national assembly. They picked the spot because the **Lögberg** ("Law Rock") cliff wall **carried the spoken law** across the valley.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
en: They chose this ground carefully: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: Standing at Lögberg. This is the exact ground where it was decided.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: Most national religions are imposed by kings or won by armies. Iceland's was decided **on this rock, by a man having a lie-down.**

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: Calmly, collectively, and after a really good night's sleep. That is how Iceland became Christian — standing where you are standing. Most countries were not given the option.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: The Day Iceland Changed Religion, Lying Down

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: By **999** the country was split — Christian districts against pagan strongholds — and Norway's King **Ólafur Tryggvason** was squeezing hard: he welcomed Christian traders into his ports, barred the pagans, and **held Icelandic hostages** as leverage. Convert, or lose the trade route you cannot live without.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: Persuasion had gone badly. One Saxon priest, **Þangbrandur**, allegedly **fought duels and killed poets** who mocked his sermons. Not a charm offensive.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: By **AD 1000** (the sources wobble between 999 and 1000) the **Alþingi** met on this spot facing two religions, two law codes and one looming civil war — so both sides handed the verdict to one man: **Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði**, the *pagan* Law-Speaker.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: He lay down under his cloak **a full day and a night**, then stood up on this rock and ruled: **one law, one people, one faith — Christianity** — so the young commonwealth would not split in two. Private sacrifice, horse-meat and infant exposure were quietly tolerated at first, then dropped. Food is food.

ctx: gloss for the name "Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka
en: the pagan Law-Speaker who lay under his cloak a day and a night, then chose Christianity

ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: The white church and the five-gabled farmhouse on your right, at the bottom of the wall.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: A thousand-year-old church, a Prime Minister's summer house, and a national shrine containing two poets — one of whom may not be the right man.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: They built this to hold the greatest Icelanders who ever lived. Two people went in. Then everyone thought about it a bit more and decided, actually, we'd rather be buried at home.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: A Westminster Abbey With Two Occupants

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: The church first went up around **1017**, the present building dates from **1859**, and the bell tower was added in **1907** — the date is on the weather vane. It has no resident priest; the one who serves it **comes out from Skálholt**, which we pass later today.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: The five-gabled farmhouse beside it is **Þingvallabær**, built in **1930** for the Alþingi millennium festival by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, the state architect. He turned its face deliberately toward **Almannagjá** — the older turf farmhouse it replaced had looked out at the lake. It began with **three gables**; two more were added after a **1970 fire** destroyed the king's house next door. Since **1974** it has been the **Prime Minister's summer residence.** One gable belongs to the church.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: Behind the church is **Skáldareitur**, the poets' plot — and it exists because of an argument over a corpse. When **Einar Benediktsson** died in **January 1940**, his ex-wife and his companion could not agree who had the right to bury him. **Jónas Jónsson frá Hriflu** saw the opening and proposed a national honour ground here, modelled on **Westminster Abbey**. Einar went into it on **27 January 1940**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: The second and last arrival was **Jónas Hallgrímsson**, Iceland's national poet, who had died in Copenhagen on **26 May 1845** of blood poisoning after breaking his leg on a staircase. His bones came home and were buried here on **16 November 1946** — over the objection of the man who dug them up, who wanted him in **Öxnadalur** where he was born. The Prime Minister, **Ólafur Thors**, overruled him. The government's position was that **Jónas's bones were state property.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: And nobody is sure they are his. Two other people had been buried on top of him in **1875** and **1900**, and both had to be lifted out first. The doubt has never gone away — there are still calls to open the grave and test what is in it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: Two graves. That is the whole national pantheon. **Halldór Laxness**, whose house we passed this morning, is not here. **Kjarval**, who opened this tour, is not here either. Iceland built itself a Westminster Abbey and then quietly stopped using it.

ctx: gloss for the name "Þingvallabær" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
en: the five-gabled farmhouse, the Prime Minister's summer residence

ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: Follow the Öxará. The waterfall ahead, the still green pool below it, and the coin-filled crack by the bridge.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: The law was spoken up on the rock. It was carried out down here, in the water.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: People throw coins in and make a wish because a sign in the 1930s told them to. Icelanders have been quietly watching tourists do it ever since and saying nothing.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: The Waterfall, the Drowning Pool and the Fake Wishing Well

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: The **Öxará** comes over the wall at **Öxarárfoss** and runs down through the assembly ground. It is the main open river feeding the whole valley — and it is doing a job it was very probably given, diverted to bring water to the assembly.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: Below the falls the river widens into a still green pool: **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**; women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** were **drowned here**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749.** A memorial plaque now names them. Two weeks a year this place made the law. It also carried out the sentence.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: And then there is **Peningagjá** — the crack full of coins by the bridge, properly the southern end of **Nikulásargjá**. The coins have nothing to do with the sagas. The **bridge went up in 1907** for the visit of the Danish king **Frederick VIII**, who is said to have thrown the first one in.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
en: The wish came later, and from a signpost. In the **1930s** somebody put up a board reading **"to the wishing well"** — and that is the entire origin of the tradition. The national park's own record is blunt about it: **no older Icelandic folk tale or story about wishing here exists.** An ancient custom, ninety years old, invented by signage.

en: the waterfall coming over the rift wall

ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: The lake filling the rift ahead of you, and the clear pools off to the side.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: Two continents pulling apart, the cleanest drinking water on the planet running through the gap, and a fish quietly turning into four other fish while nobody watches.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: Iceland's answer to a tectonic disaster: turn it into a reservoir, then drink it.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: The Cleanest Water on Earth, and Four Fish That Are One Fish

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: **Þingvallavatn** is Iceland's largest natural lake: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, averaging **34 m**, sitting at roughly **100.5 m above sea level** — and its bed lies **below sea level** because of the rifting.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: About **nine-tenths of everything entering it arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava at **3–4°C**. Only about a tenth comes in as visible surface water, most of that the **Öxará**. The catchment runs to some **1,300 km²**, of which the lake is only about **six per cent** — the rest is plumbing you cannot see.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces. Clear pools like **Silfra** are that meltwater arriving. The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years.** **Kuðungableikja**, the snail charr. **Dvergbleikja**, the dwarf. **Murta**, the small open-water one. **Sílableikja**, the fish-eater. Two feed on the bottom, two feed in open water — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: **Three of the four are genetically distinct.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out muddled — some read as murta, others as crosses. Vísindavefurinn's assessment is that this may be **sympatric speciation**, one population dividing with no physical barrier between the halves, and that another **10,000 years** could produce genuinely separate species. Evolution has not finished tidying up.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: That island out in the lake is **Sandey**, a **tuff cone** built by **Hengill** about **1,900 years ago** — the same eruption that laid down **Nesjahraun** at the north end. An eruption happened in the middle of a lake and built itself an island out of it.

ctx: gloss for the name "Langjökull" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: the glacier the water left 30 to 100 years ago

ctx: gloss for the name "murta" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: the small open-water charr, one of the lake's four forms

ctx: gloss for the name "Sandey" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
en: the tuff-cone island Hengill built about 1,900 years ago

ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: Back at the Law Rock. This is where the country stopped belonging to anybody else.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: A thousand years after the first assembly, on the same ground, the country finished the job.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: It absolutely poured. Tens of thousands stood in it for hours. If you want one image of how much this particular field means to Icelanders — that is the one.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: The Republic, in the Rain

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: They could have done it in Reykjavík, in a building, dry. They chose this ground instead: **the place the nation first assembled in 930**, and the place Denmark had shut down in **1800**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: The date was not an accident either — **17 June** is the birthday of **Jón Sigurðsson**, the man who led the independence campaign and who did not live to see it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
en: It rained. It rained hard, the whole way through. Nobody left. The photographs of that day are mostly a valley full of soaked people refusing to go home.

en: the independence leader whose birthday, 17 June, became the national day

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is nearly the newest thing you'll touch today. The transport minister cut the ribbon on **Friday 2 November 2001**, standing down at Selvallavatn where we're headed, and the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass was retired that same day after generations of hauling traffic over the peninsula's spine. **16.4 km** of new road, topping out at **230 m** against Kerlingarskarð's **311 m** — and only **3 km** of it above 200 metres, where the old road had **ten**. We replaced the pass, not the mountains.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: Down in the bogs at the south end of **Sátudalur** two streams rise almost side by side and then immediately fall out. **Rauðusteinalækur** runs south into Baulárvallavatn and eventually reaches the sea as Straumfjarðará. **Fossá** runs north, over the waterfall we're stopping at — and then vanishes completely. I'll show you where in about ten minutes.

ctx: block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: 💧 Fossá

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: At the Vatnaleið viewpoint — the fall is below the road, the lake beyond it.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: The postcard version gives you a name, a height and a river. **All three are wrong.** What's actually here is better: the one waterfall in a country of obsessive namers that nobody could be bothered to name.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: Land the punchline slowly: the National Land Survey maps this fall, and leaves the name field blank. Let that sit for a beat before you move to the lake.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: The Waterfall Iceland Never Bothered to Name

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: Start with the river, because the internet gets this wrong constantly. This is **Fossá** — literally *"waterfall river."* It is **not** Straumfjarðará. Straumfjarðará rises in Baulárvallavatn, back the way we came, and runs the opposite direction to the sea at Straumfjörður. Different river, different catchment, different ocean-facing coast.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: **Landmælingar Íslands**, the National Land Survey, has this fall in its database. Mapped, plotted, classified as *foss*. The name field is **blank**. Náttúrufræðistofnun holds the same point, also blank.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: So I went looking. **Zero** hits for "Selvallafoss" in Árnastofnun's national place-name archive. **Zero** in the national mapping database — the only "Selval-" name in the whole country is the lake. **Zero** across the entire Icelandic newspaper corpus, which runs back well over two hundred years. "Selvallavatn" gets 71 hits. The waterfall gets none.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: Meanwhile the place-name survey of the farm above us lists **Steinkarl**, **Nóngjá**, **Krummaklettar**, **Stóriklettur** — *"where the hidden people sang."* Seventy-nine names. They named a rock for its singing elves and left the waterfall alone.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: I think the old answer was just simpler than ours: the river was **already** called *the waterfall river*. Naming the waterfall on the waterfall river is like opening a restaurant called Restaurant.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: And no — **nobody has ever officially measured its height.** No figure in the national survey, none in the natural history institute, none in *Íslenskir fossar*, the standard reference on Icelandic waterfalls, which records two other falls in this district and skips this one. Every number you'll find online was typed by somebody with a website and a deadline. I'd rather give you nothing than give you a number I can't stand behind.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: One last thing while we're demolishing: **sel** does not mean sheep, and it does not mean seal. A *sel* is a **shieling** — the summer dairy station where the milking animals went up the valley. **Selvellir** means *"the shieling flats."* In the **1700s** the farm Horn was split in two, and the new half was built on Horn's old shieling ground. The farm went empty in the **1920s** and never came back.

en: "waterfall river"; the river the fall is actually on

ctx: gloss for the name "Selvellir" — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: "the shieling flats"; the deserted farm above us

ctx: gloss for the name "sel" — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: a shieling, the summer dairy station. Not a sheep. Not a seal.

ctx: gloss for the name "Landmælingar Íslands" — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: the National Land Survey, which maps the fall with no name

ctx: gloss for the name "Straumfjarðará" — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá
en: the river this one is not

ctx: block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: 🌀 Selvallavatn

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: Same viewpoint — the lake in the hollow between the lava and the mountain wall.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: A lake fed by a river, sitting on porous lava, with **no way out** — and the only candidate explanation is a whirlpool a farm boy noticed and nobody ever followed up.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: The "perhaps" is the whole block. Deliver it as an open question, not a solved one — because it is one.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: The Lake With No Way Out

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: **Selvallavatn** sits at **62 metres** above sea level in a hollow between Berserkjahraun and the mountain wall. Fossá runs in on the east, small becks run in on the south. And that is the entire hydrological story, because there is **no outflow above ground.** None.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: The man who wrote down the place-names here was **Lárus Halldórsson**, born on the farm above us in **1920**. Going back over the survey he added a feature the earlier recorder had missed: **Rás** — a swallow-hole at the lava's edge *"where the water is sucked in a whirlpool down into the lava."* Then he added one careful sentence: **perhaps that is the answer to the riddle of Selvallavatn's outflow.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: *Perhaps.* He left it open. And as far as I can find, in the eighty-odd years since, **nobody has closed it.** No dye trace, no survey, no paper. A lake disappearing into a lava field, and the last word on it is a farmer's son saying "maybe."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: It hasn't always been Selvallavatn either. The old name in the record is **Svínavatn** — *pig lake.* Less romantic, and it clearly lost the marketing meeting.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: There's **brown trout and Arctic charr** in it — the trout run a solid **three to six pounds**, and on summer evenings shoals of small charr work along the lava edge. In a dry spell the water level can drop by **a metre and a half**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: How big is it? Genuinely nobody agrees. The standard Icelandic reference says **0.85 km²**. The national mapping database maps the shoreline at **0.30 km²**. That is a factor of nearly three, on a lake you can see the whole of from here, and I am not going to pretend I can settle it. **Maximum depth: never surveyed at all.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: The lay-by you are standing on isn't an accident, by the way. When Vatnaleið was built, an **architect** was brought in to design this viewpoint — and in **2003** the whole road took **Vegagerðin's first-ever award** for construction and finish, with the jury singling out this spot. Congratulations. You are standing on an award-winning lay-by.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn
en: The lake, Berserkjahraun and the neighbouring waters are all on the **Náttúruminjaskrá**, Iceland's nature conservation register, as item **227**.
